highlights.title: Free and open source, as the way people found it
highlights.text: Anyone can run Postiz free on their own server. People who don't want the hassle pay $29+ a month for the hosted version. Every small feature shipped as a new release, and every release was a reason to post on Hacker News, Reddit and Dev.to.
highlights.quote: "Charge only for cloud costs, never force developers to pay."
highlights.label: Claimed

highlights.title: Plugging into the AI agent wave early
highlights.text: Postiz shipped an n8n integration, then an MCP server, a command-line tool and an OpenClaw skill, so AI agents could post through Postiz by default. When OpenClaw went viral in early 2026 and someone else's article about it used Postiz, signups jumped. Revenue grew from $21K to $118K a month in about three months.
highlights.label: Claimed

phases.name: Before Postiz
phases.story: The founder was a growth marketer at Novu, another open-source company (it shares its code free for anyone to use), where the project grew to 30,000 GitHub stars (like bookmarks on GitHub, the site where code is shared) in two years. His first solo product, Gitroom, made some money but "the market was tiny". He dropped it after about six months.
phases.lesson: Start where you already understand how people find things. Drop a product quickly when the market is too small.
phases.title: Before Postiz: a tiny market, dropped fast
phases.dek: He learned how open-source projects get found at another company. His first product of his own made some money, but the market was too small, so he stopped after about six months.

phases.name: Building
phases.story: Postiz started as a regular social media scheduler for creators, businesses and agencies. He spent about $12,000 on SEO articles (articles meant to rank on Google) for a brand-new website. They brought almost no traffic, and he stopped.

number.v: July 2024 homepage: "Your ultimate social media scheduling tool." Nothing that stood out from Buffer or Hootsuite yet.
number.label: Claimed

phases.lesson: A new domain has no authority with Google. Paying for SEO in month one is usually money gone.
phases.title: Building: $12K on SEO that didn't work
phases.dek: Postiz started as a regular scheduler that looked like Buffer or Hootsuite. He paid for SEO articles on a brand-new site, got almost no traffic, and cut the channel.

receipts.caption: postiz.com in July 2024: "Your ultimate social media scheduling tool"
receipts.label: Wayback

phases.name: Open source
phases.story:
In September 2024 he made Postiz open source: anyone could read the code, run it on their own server for free, or pay to use the hosted version.

Then he ran launch weeks on Hacker News, Reddit, Dev.to and Product Hunt (sites where people share new projects), all aimed at one goal: GitHub's trending page, where developers look for new projects.

Reddit users kept asking for a Docker setup, an easy way to install it on a server. He built it. GitHub stars went from about 3,000 to 14,000 in three months.

number.v: Revenue went from about $700 a month to $6.5K by July 2025 and $14K by November 2025. Over a year of slow growth.
number.label: Claimed

phases.lesson: Free gets attention, but attention is not revenue. Expect a long stretch where the free version grows and the paid version barely moves.
phases.title: Open source: free gets attention, not revenue
phases.dek: He gave the code away, ran launch weeks and climbed GitHub. Stars grew fast. The money took more than a year to follow.
phases.why: Stars proved people wanted it. They didn't prove people would pay. If you give something away, decide in advance how long you can keep going while it stays flat.

receipts.label: Claimed
receipts.text: Users asked for a Docker setup, so he built one.

steal.title: Steal this: his launch-week checklist
items: Make the free version easy to install. He added Docker when Reddit asked.
Pick your launch sites. His were Hacker News, Reddit, Dev.to and Product Hunt.
Aim every post at one goal. His was GitHub's trending page.
Decide how many months you can keep going while revenue stays flat.

phases.name: Finding the users who stay
phases.story:
He noticed people using Postiz inside n8n automations (n8n connects apps so tasks run by themselves) and YouTube tutorials about automating social media. He published an official n8n node, improved the public API (the way other software talks to Postiz), messaged Skool communities (paid online groups) to promote Postiz, and started an affiliate program (people who bring in customers get a cut) paying about 30% every month for as long as the customer stays.

His reasoning: people posting by hand cancel, but "when people are posting with automation, that's a whole different story."
phases.lesson: Look at who your most active users are, then build for them.
phases.title: Finding the users who stay: build for the automators
phases.dek: People were posting through Postiz from n8n automations. He built an n8n node, a better API and an affiliate program for them, because people who automate their posting tend to stay.

phases.name: The turning point
phases.story: OpenClaw, an AI agent project, went viral. Postiz was ready with an MCP server (a way for AI agents to use Postiz), a command-line tool (you control it by typing commands) and an OpenClaw skill. A third-party writer published a popular article about an agent that posted TikTok slideshows through Postiz.

number.v: Reported: $21K a month in March 2026, $80K in April, $118K in June, $145K on July 2.
number.label: Claimed

phases.lesson: You can't plan a viral moment, but you can be the tool that's ready when one happens.
phases.title: The turning point: ready when AI agents went viral
phases.dek: When OpenClaw went viral, Postiz already had an MCP server, a command-line tool and an OpenClaw skill. A popular article used Postiz, and signups jumped.

receipts.caption: postiz.com today: "Run your social media on autopilot with" AI agents like ChatGPT
receipts.label: Live

phases.name: Scaling the content
phases.story: A weekly system on X: a Monday video that is useful on its own and only mentions Postiz, clips of it all week, then the same idea as a long X article the next week. He replies to every comment, and runs daily short videos through creators, where he says about 1 in 30 takes off.
phases.lesson: One idea, repackaged several times, beats new content every day.
phases.title: Scaling the content: one idea, packaged many ways
phases.dek: A weekly system on X turns one useful video into clips and a long article, and creators post short videos every day.

checklist.text: Pick one place your users already hang out and post there every time you ship something, even small updates.
Give something away free and charge for the convenient version, the way Postiz is free to self-host and paid to use hosted.
Build a plug-in for a tool that's growing fast right now, like AI agents or n8n. It's cheap for one person and puts you where new users are looking.
Find your most active users and build for them. Postiz followed the automation crowd instead of competing with Buffer.
Don't pay for SEO on a brand-new site. Write a few useful posts yourself and spend the money elsewhere.
Plan for a long flat stretch. Postiz stayed under $15K a month for about 14 months after going open source. Pace yourself around school.
